Tullock Creek was called by the Crows "Where Many Colts Died" because once when some Crows were camped here a severe hail storm came and killed many young horses. The Crow name for Sarpy Creek is "Where White Flanked Horses are Caught". It was said that in the early 1900's a herd of stray horses roamed here with many having distinctive white markings on the flanks. These were apparently well bred animals and Crows often captured these "slicks" and tamed them as saddle horses.
Meanwhile, the white settlers recognized that the area east of the Little Big Horn and the lower Big Horn Rivers was perfect for livestock grazing. As early as 1890, large sheep and cattle companies and individual ranchers were on the reservation competing for grazing permits.
By an agreement made on August 14, 1899, the Crow Indians agreed to sell about 1,150,000 acres of the reservation to the government for $5.00 per acre. However, when the Agreement was enacted into legislation on April 27, 1904 (33 Stat. 352) the direct purchase arrangement was deleted. Instead the Government would act as a real estate agent for the tribe:
"It is the intent of this act that the U.S. shall act as trustee for said Crow Indians to dispose of the ceded lands and pay over the proceeds from the sale thereof only as received. That nothing in this act shall bind the U.S. to purchase lands not claimed or to guarantee to find purchasers".
Indians living on the ceded lands were permitted to remain and receive allotments on the lands they were occuping, or to move to the reduced reservation and receive payment for their former lands and the improvements thereon.
